parts.title: UPSC History: Gandhi's Arrival & Early Satyagrahas
parts.intro: Today we study the 'Entry of the Mahatma'. After two decades in South Africa, M.K. Gandhi returned to India in 1915. He didn't join politics immediately; instead, he traveled and tested his weapon of 'Satyagraha' (Truth-Force) in three localized struggles: Champaran, Kheda, and Ahmedabad. These 'Triple Victories' established him as a leader of the masses. For UPSC, mastering the 'Sequence' and 'Issues' of these three struggles is a Prelims favorite. Let's trace the birth of Gandhian politics today.

blocks.text: Workers demanded restoration of a 'Plague Bonus' withdrawn by mill owners. Gandhi's hunger strike forced an agreement, marking the first use of fasting for a labor cause in India.

parts.title: UPSC History: Non-Cooperation & Chauri Chaura
parts.intro: Today we study the 'First Mass Strike'. The Non-Cooperation Movement (NCM) was Gandhi's first pan-India struggle, launched in 1920 to undo the 'Punjab Wrongs' and support the Khilafat cause. It saw the surrender of titles, boycott of schools, and the rise of the 'Charkha'. For UPSC, focus on the 'Program of NCM' and the controversial withdrawal after the 'Chauri Chaura' incident. This movement changed the nature of the Indian freedom struggle forever.

pages.title: Launch of NCM (1920)
pages.intro: Nationwide protest approved at Nagpur Congress (Dec 1920) to achieve Swaraj through non-cooperation.

pages.title: Program of Action
pages.intro: Gandhi-led activities (1920-22) urging Indians to boycott British institutions and adopt swadeshi alternatives.

items.label: Surrender titles
items.value: e.g., Kaiser-i-Hind medal returned by Gandhi

pages.title: Chauri Chaura (Feb 5, 1922)
pages.intro: Violent clash in Gorakhpur (UP) where protesters burned a police station, killing 22 policemen.

blocks.text: Gandhi called off the Non-Cooperation Movement immediately after this incident, proving his absolute commitment to non-violence.

pages.title: Impact of Withdrawal
pages.intro: NCM withdrawal in 1922 shocked leaders, caused a lull, and led to internal divisions among nationalists.

rows: Shock; Bose called it a 'national calamity'

pages.title: Economic Impact
pages.intro: Swadeshi Movement halved British cloth imports, boosting Indian textile mills and handlooms.

blocks.text: Foreign cloth = textiles made outside India, mainly Britain. Demand surged for Indian mill-made and handloom cloth.

parts.title: UPSC History: Civil Disobedience & Salt Satyagraha
parts.intro: Today we study the 'Great Defiance'. The Civil Disobedience Movement (CDM) began with the iconic Dandi March in 1930. By picking up a handful of salt, Gandhi challenged the moral authority of the British Empire. This movement saw unprecedented mass participation, especially from women and business classes. For UPSC, focus on the 'Dandi Route', the 'Gandhi-Irwin Pact', and the various regional centers like Dharasana and Vedaranyam. This was the moment the world watched India.

pages.title: Purna Swaraj Declaration (1929)
pages.intro: The Purna Swaraj Declaration, meaning "Complete Self-Rule," was a formal announcement made by the Indian National Congress (INC), the main political party fighting for India's freedom from British rule, during its annual meeting in Lahore in December 1929. The president of this session was Jawaharlal Nehru, who later became India's first Prime Minister. At this meeting, the Congress changed its official goal from demanding "Dominion Status," which meant self-rule while still recognizing the British King, to demanding "Purna Swaraj," or complete and total independence from Britain. To show their commitment, the Congress declared that January 26, 1930, would be celebrated as the first Independence Day across India, where people would take a public pledge to fight for full freedom. This declaration was a major turning point because it rejected any compromise with British rule and set the clear, non-negotiable goal of complete independence for the country.

pages.title: Dandi March (March 12 - April 6, 1930)
pages.intro: The Dandi March was a 241-mile walk led by Mahatma Gandhi, accompanied by 78 of his followers, from his ashram in Sabarmati to the coastal village of Dandi in Gujarat. This march was a deliberate act of civil disobedience, which means the peaceful refusal to obey an unjust law, specifically targeting the British salt law. The British salt law was a government rule that made it illegal for Indians to make or sell their own salt, forcing them to buy heavily taxed, British-controlled salt instead. When Gandhi and his followers reached Dandi on April 6, 1930, they openly violated the law by picking up natural salt from the seashore. This single act signaled the beginning of the Civil Disobedience Movement (CDM), which was a nationwide campaign of nonviolent resistance against British rule.

pages.title: Regional Movements
pages.intro: Regional movements were part of the Civil Disobedience Movement started by Mahatma Gandhi in 1930 to break the British salt law. In Tamil Nadu, C. Rajagopalachari led a march from Trichy to Vedaranyam to make salt illegally. In the Malabar region of Kerala, K. Kelappan led a similar salt march. In Peshawar, now in Pakistan, Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, called the Frontier Gandhi, led a nonviolent group known as the Khudai Khidmatgar, meaning servants of God. At Dharasana in Gujarat, Sarojini Naidu led a protest raid on the salt works. These actions spread the independence movement across different parts of India.

blocks.text: Note: Bhagat Singh's execution was NOT stayed.

pages.title: Features of CDM
pages.intro: The Civil Disobedience Movement, or CDM, was a major campaign of nonviolent protest against British rule in India, launched in 1930. Unlike earlier movements, it involved the deliberate violation of specific British laws, such as the salt law which made it illegal for Indians to make or sell salt, not just refusing to cooperate with the government. A key feature was the massive participation of women, who came out in large numbers to picket shops selling foreign cloth and liquor, breaking traditional social barriers. The movement also included a boycott of foreign cloth and liquor, meaning people refused to buy or use these items to hurt British economic interests. Additionally, there were no-tax and no-rent campaigns, where peasants and farmers refused to pay taxes or rent to the British authorities and landlords, challenging the economic foundation of colonial rule.

parts.title: UPSC History: Quit India Movement & INA
parts.intro: Today we study the 'Final Blow'. The Quit India Movement (1942) was the most violent and spontaneous mass uprising since 1857. With the slogan 'Do or Die', Gandhi gave a clarion call for the British to leave immediately. Simultaneously, Subhas Chandra Bose led the Indian National Army (INA) from outside. For UPSC, focus on the 'Underground activities' of leaders like Usha Mehta and the significance of the 'Parallel Governments'. This is the endgame of the Raj.
